''Ophiopogon spicatus'' var. ''kunthianus'' Maxim. }} '''''Liriope muscari''''' is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] [[native plant|from]] [[East Asia]]. Common names in English include '''big blue lilyturf''', '''lilyturf''', '''border grass''', and '''monkey grass'''. This small [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] has grass-like [[evergreen]] foliage and lilac-purple flowers which produce single-seeded berries on a spike in the fall. In some parts of the United States, it is an [[invasive species]].{{Cite web |title=monkeygrass: Liriope muscari (Asparagales: Asparagaceae): Invasive Plant Atlas of the United States |url=https://www.invasiveplantatlas.org/subject.html?sub=11612 |access-date=2026-05-03 |website=www.invasiveplantatlas.org}} ==Description== It is an [[Understory|understory plant]] in China, Japan, and Korea occurring in shady forests at elevations of {{convert|330|-|4600|ft|m|0|abbr=on}}.[https://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Liriope+muscari Plants for a Future: ''Liriope muscari''.] It typically grows {{convert|30|-|45|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall and features clumps of strap-like, arching, glossy, dark green leaves to ½ inch wide (1.3 cm).[http://hort.ufl.edu/shrubs/LIRMUSA.PDF Edward F. Gilman 1999. ''Liriope muscari''. University of Florida: Cooperative Extension Service. Fact Sheet FPS 347.] Clumps slowly expand by short stolons to a width of about {{convert|30|cm|0|abbr=on}}, but plants do not spread aggressively. Roots are fibrous, often with terminal tubers. The small, showy flowers occur on erect spikes with tiered whorls of dense, white to violet-purple flowers rising above the leaves in late summer. Flowers resemble those of grape hyacinth (''[[Muscari]]''), which is the origin of the [[specific epithet]]. Flowers develop into blackish berries which often persist into winter. Lilyturf is deer resistant. There is considerable variation in leaf color and size among a number of recognized cultivars. ===Distinguishing characteristics=== Distinguishing species in the genus ''Liriope'' is difficult at best, and mistaken identity occurs in commercial nurseries.{{Cite web |url=http://etd.lsu.edu/docs/available/etd-04102007-113758/unrestricted/Broussard_dis.pdf |title=Mary C. Broussard. 2007. A Horticultural Study of ''Liriope'' and ''Ophiopogon'': Nomenclature, Morphology and Culture. Louisiana State University. Dissertation. 129 p. |access-date=2009-07-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100719044529/http://etd.lsu.edu/docs/available/etd-04102007-113758/unrestricted/Broussard_dis.pdf |archive-date=2010-07-19 |url-status=dead }} ''L. muscari'' is distinguished from ''[[Liriope spicata]]'', the other most common species in the genus, by its fibrous rather than [[rhizome|rhizomatous]] root system, its more prominent flower spike extending above the leaves (creeping lilyturf has a shorter spike more within leaves), and its generally wider and longer leaves. ==Cultivation== Landscape uses include borders (along sidewalks, trails, driveways, shrubbery, and trees) and mass plantings as [[groundcover]]. Lilyturf can be established on steep slopes where erosion control is needed. Minimal maintenance is required. The species is easily grown in average, medium, well-drained soils in full sun to part shade. Ideal conditions are moist, fertile soils with partial shade. However, lilyturf tolerates a wide range of light and soil conditions. Lilyturf is also tolerant of heat, humidity, and drought. The evergreen foliage often turns brown in late winter; old foliage can be cut back or mowed at a high setting before new shoots appear in early spring. Lilyturf is suitable for [[USDA Hardiness Zone]]s 6 to 10. It might be grown in zone 5 in sheltered locations or if protected during severe winter weather. Being an easy plant to grow, it is one of the most popular groundcovers in the southeastern United States and areas with a similar climate, and is commonly used in [[gardening|landscaping]] in temperate climates as border plants and groundcover. It is classified as an invasive species in some parts of the eastern United States. Native plants such as [[Florida gamagrass]],[https://www.abettersouthflorida.org/go-native/ Go Native: Dwarf gamma grass vs Liriope.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090310172240/http://www.abettersouthflorida.org/GoNative/gammavliriope.htm |date=2009-03-10 }} [[Carex plantaginea|seersucker sedge]], and [[phlox]] are alternatives that offer more value to wildlife.{{Cite web |last=Michetti |first=Jess |date=2023-02-27 |title=Plant This, Not That: Replacing Liriope |url=https://www.nvbirdalliance.org/news/plant-this-not-that-march-2023 |access-date=2026-05-03 |website=Northern Virginia Bird Alliance |language=en-US}} In the [[United Kingdom]] ''Liriope muscari'' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Liriope muscari''|url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/10344/liriope-muscari/details |access-date=13 October 2022}}{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 61 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 25 March 2018}} ===Propagation=== [[Image:Liriope muscari seeds.jpg|right|thumb|Seeds]] ====Seeds==== The plant is difficult to reproduce from seed due to several factors.[http://www.uky.edu/Ag/HLA/Geneve/teaching/PLS%20440/Labs/posterexample.pdf John Jones; Sarah White. Seeds of ''Liriope muscari'' Require Warm Stratification for Germination. University of Kentucky, College of Agriculture, Department of Horticulture.] The fruit's pulp contains [[polyphenol|phenolic]] compounds that inhibit germination, and thus need to be removed to promote germination. In addition, seeds have a [[seeds#Seed dormancy|morphological dormancy]] because the embryo is not fully developed when the fruit ripens; a period of warm stratification is required to complete maturation. Lastly, the seeds do not store well. Cleaned seeds can be sown outdoors after the fruit ripens in early fall, recognizing that germination will be slow the following spring. Rapid germination can be promoted by warm, moist stratification of cleaned seed under dark conditions for 8 weeks at 77 degrees F (25 degrees C) for optimum germination.[https://www.actahort.org/books/517/517_8.htm T. Shimomura, T. Kondo 2000. Seed Germination and Polyembryony of some Liliaceae Ground Covers Native to Japan. Horticulturae 517.] Stratified seeds can be started indoors or in a heated greenhouse during the dormant season or they may be sown outdoors after the threat of frost has passed. ====Division==== Lilyturf is easily reproduced by dividing the root mass. The optimum time to do this is during the dormant season before the onset of new growth. Plants produced by division are identical to the mother plant; thus cultivar traits will be retained. ===Problems=== No serious diseases or pests occur for cultivated ''Liriope muscari''. Root rot (''[[Pythium]]'') has been reported. [[Anthracnose]] fungus sometimes causes reddish streaks in the leaves. [[Scale insect]]s have been reported to cause unsightly reddish spots on leaves during late summer. Slugs and snails are occasional pests.[https://www.ctahr.hawaii.edu/oc/freepubs/pdf/liriope.pdf Jay Deputy. 1999. Liriope, the “Other” Mondo Grass. College of Tropical Agriculture & Human Resources, University of Hawaii at Manona: Cooperative Extension Service.] ==Other uses== The roots, which often have fleshy tubers near their tip, are used in [[traditional Chinese medicine]]. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Other online resources== {{commons category}} *[http://www.mobot.org/GARDENINGHELP/PLANTFINDER/plant.asp?code=L100 Missouri Botanical Garden: Kemper Center for Home Gardening: ''Liriope muscari''.] *[http://www.fandistrict.org/FDAsite/Liriope.htm Fan District Association of Richmond, Virginia: Everything you wanted to know about ground cover in the tree out front--Liriope.]{{dead link|date=December 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} {{Taxonbar|from=Q141540}} [[Category:Convallarioideae]] [[Category:Flora of Asia]] [[Category:Plants used in traditional Chinese medicine]] [[Category:Garden plants of Asia]] [[Category:Groundcovers]] [[Category:Taxa named by Joseph Decaisne]]
